q: מהו תומך בקבלת החלטות לפי חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות?
o: אפוטרופוס המקבל החלטות במקום האדם מכוח מינוי שיפוטי ובהתאם לסמכויות שנקבעו
אדם הממונה לסייע בקבלת החלטות מבלי להחליף את שיקול דעתו של האדם
עורך דין שמחליט במקום האדם על הטיפול הרפואי משום שהוא מייצג אותו בהליך המשפטי
עובד סוציאלי שמקבל את ההחלטה הסופית במקום האדם לאחר שהסביר לו את החלופות
explanation:
**תמיכה בקבלת החלטות** מסייעת לקבל מידע, להבין חלופות ולממש החלטות, אך **ההחלטה נשארת בידי האדם** (סעיף 67ב, עמ׳ 61 ו־62 בקובץ). בית המשפט רשאי למנות תומך לבגיר שיכול לקבל החלטות בעצמו בעזרת תמיכה; הסיוע אינו מעביר לתומך את שיקול הדעת (סעיף 67ב(ד), עמ׳ 62).
"תומך בקבלת החלטות לא יקבל החלטות בשמו של האדם שהוא מסייע לו." (עמ׳ 62 (PDF)).

**א. אפוטרופוס המקבל החלטות במקום האדם מכוח מינוי שיפוטי ובהתאם לסמכויות שנקבעו.** שגויה, קבלת החלטות במקום האדם היא תפקיד מחליף, ואילו לתומך נאסר לקבל החלטות בשם האדם (סעיף 67ב(ג), עמ׳ 62).
**ב. אדם הממונה לסייע בקבלת החלטות מבלי להחליף את שיקול דעתו של האדם.** נכונה, התומך מסייע בהבנת המידע ובמימוש ההחלטות בלי להפוך לבעל ההחלטה; זה המבנה שנקבע בחוק (סעיף 67ב, עמ׳ 61 ו־62).
**ג. עורך דין שמחליט במקום האדם על הטיפול הרפואי משום שהוא מייצג אותו בהליך המשפטי.** שגויה, ייצוג מקצועי אינו מתיר לתומך להחליט במקום האדם; כיישום האיסור, הוא חל גם אם התומך הוא עורך דין (סעיף 67ב(ג), עמ׳ 62).
**ד. עובד סוציאלי שמקבל את ההחלטה הסופית במקום האדם לאחר שהסביר לו את החלופות.** שגויה, הסבר חלופות הוא סיוע מתאים, אך החלטה סופית במקום האדם חורגת מתפקיד התומך (סעיף 67ב(א) ו־(ג), עמ׳ 61 ו־62).

מקור: חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ_ב-1962.pdf עמ׳ 61 בקובץ; חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ_ב-1962.pdf עמ׳ 62 בקובץ.
label: Source: חוק הכשרות המשפטית והאפוטרופסות, תשכ״ב-1962 · §67ב; PDF pp61–62

q: A 69-year-old man is found to have new anemia on routine testing. There are currently no findings suggesting a hematologic malignancy, and no etiologic work-up has been performed. Which group of tests belongs in the initial evaluation described by Hazzard?
o: Blood count and reticulocytes, followed by marrow aspiration and biopsy to identify hematologic disease
Blood count and reticulocytes, iron and vitamin studies, and renal, thyroid, and liver tests
Erythropoietin, copper, zinc, and C-reactive protein measurements to investigate additional causes
Serum protein electrophoresis, lactate dehydrogenase, and haptoglobin measurements to investigate additional causes
explanation:
**Initial investigations** target common causes of anemia before moving to less common explanations. The source lists blood count, reticulocytes, ferritin, iron studies, creatinine, vitamin B12, red-cell folate, thyroid tests, and liver tests, explaining that they "help clinicians rule out the most common causes of anemia" (p. 1480). Additional studies follow when that evaluation is unrevealing; marrow sampling is required when a hematologic malignancy is suspected (p. 1480).

**A. Blood count and reticulocytes, followed by marrow aspiration and biopsy to identify hematologic disease.** Wrong, blood count and reticulocytes are initial tests, but marrow aspiration and biopsy are tied to suspicion of hematologic malignancy, which is not stated here (p. 1480).
**B. Blood count and reticulocytes, iron and vitamin studies, and renal, thyroid, and liver tests.** Correct, this group matches the source's initial assessment for nutritional, renal, and other common contributors to anemia (p. 1480).
**C. Erythropoietin, copper, zinc, and C-reactive protein measurements to investigate additional causes.** Wrong, these are listed among further investigations when the initial tests are unrevealing, rather than replacing that first-stage evaluation (p. 1480).
**D. Serum protein electrophoresis, lactate dehydrogenase, and haptoglobin measurements to investigate additional causes.** Wrong, these also belong to the further work-up of rarer causes after an unrevealing initial investigation (p. 1480).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1480.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Hematopoietic System and Anemia
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1480

q: An older man with glaucoma and cognitive impairment has a complex regimen of eye drops and other medications. It is unclear whether he uses them as prescribed. Which principle should guide review?
o: Clarify actual use and simplify to an effective medication regimen
Add medications from the recorded list before asking about actual use
Exclude eye drops from the review and concentrate on oral medications
Increase dosing frequency and regimen complexity to improve adherence
explanation:
**Medication review** should establish actual use and include topical preparations (p. 313). Greater complexity is associated with lower adherence and more adverse effects; the source recommends "the simplest regimen that controls the patient’s symptoms and illnesses" (p. 313).

**A. Clarify actual use and simplify to an effective medication regimen.** Correct, this addresses actual use and the source's goal of an effective, simple regimen (p. 313).
**B. Add medications from the recorded list before asking about actual use.** Wrong, adding treatment from the list without checking use omits the recommended comprehensive review (p. 313).
**C. Exclude eye drops from the review and concentrate on oral medications.** Wrong, topical agents and eye drops belong in the review rather than being excluded (p. 313).
**D. Increase dosing frequency and regimen complexity to improve adherence.** Wrong, greater complexity is associated with reduced adherence and more adverse effects, contrary to this proposal (p. 313).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 313.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: In which population was durvalumab studied in the PACIFIC trial as described in Hazzard?
o: Resectable stage III NSCLC after complete surgical resection
Stage IV NSCLC after disease control with chemotherapy
Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent chemoradiation
Unresectable stage III NSCLC after sequential chemotherapy and radiation
explanation:
**PACIFIC** studied unresectable stage III NSCLC with disease control after concurrent chemoradiation. These features define the population from which the trial evidence described on this page was obtained; applying them to identify the study population is an inference from the reported enrollment description (p. 1426). "patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC who had disease control after concurrent chemoradiation were randomized" (p. 1426).

**A. Resectable stage III NSCLC after complete surgical resection.** Wrong, the described population had unresectable disease after chemoradiation, rather than resectable disease after complete surgery (p. 1426).
**B. Stage IV NSCLC after disease control with chemotherapy.** Wrong, the reported population had stage III disease after concurrent chemoradiation, not stage IV disease after chemotherapy (p. 1426).
**C. Unresectable stage III NSCLC after concurrent chemoradiation.** Correct, this includes the reported stage, unresectability, and concurrent treatment; the source also specifies disease control before randomization (p. 1426).
**D. Unresectable stage III NSCLC after sequential chemotherapy and radiation.** Wrong, the trial description specifies concurrent chemoradiation, not sequential delivery of the two treatments (p. 1426).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1426.

q: An 80-year-old man with Parkinson disease is found confused and nearly unresponsive. Temperature is 32.5 degrees C, blood pressure 90/55, and heart rate 48. He takes carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg four times daily, pramipexole 1 mg three times daily, benztropine 1 mg twice daily, and chlorpromazine 50 mg at bedtime for chronic hiccups. Recent TSH is 4.2 and creatinine 1.8; ECG shows J waves. Rewarming has begun. Which general interpretation of medication exposure should guide the search for contributors to hypothermia?
o: Treat medication exposure as a potentially reversible contributor.
Treat medication exposure as a potential protective factor against hypothermia.
Treat medication exposure as a potential reason to discount reversible causes.
Treat medication exposure as a potential reason to defer etiologic assessment.
explanation:
**Medication exposure** belongs in the assessment of hypothermia because medicines may increase risk (p. 582). Hazzard describes "medications, which may enhance the risk of hypothermia" and calls for a comprehensive assessment of potentially reversible contributors (p. 582). The medication groups listed in Table 39-2 include phenothiazines (p. 583); this supports review, without ranking one drug withdrawal above all other interventions.

**A. Treat medication exposure as a potentially reversible contributor.** Correct, the source identifies medication exposure as a potentially reversible contributor that belongs in the assessment (pp. 582-583).
**B. Treat medication exposure as a potential protective factor against hypothermia.** Wrong, the source warns of increased hypothermia risk from medications, rather than a protective effect (p. 582).
**C. Treat medication exposure as a potential reason to discount reversible causes.** Wrong, medications are included among potentially reversible factors, rather than a reason to discount such factors (p. 583).
**D. Treat medication exposure as a potential reason to defer etiologic assessment.** Wrong, the source calls for comprehensive assessment of contributing factors, including medications, rather than deferring it because of exposure (pp. 582-583).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 582, 583.
ref: Hazzard Ch 39 — SYSTEMS PHYSIOLOGY OF AGING AND SELECTED DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTASIS

q: בן 88, סובל מפצע לחץ בטרוכנטר ימין. ראה תמונה 2. הוא מטופל בביתו ע"י משפחתו המעוניינים בטיפול האופטימלי עבור ומוכנים לקנות כל תכשיר. מה התכשיר המומלץ לניקוי הפצע לפני החלפת חבישה?
o: מי חמצן 3%
תמיסת NaCl 0.9%
מים מינרלים סטריליים
Polydin 10%
explanation:
Official answer: ב

**Official answer: ב׳** (IMA final post-appeal key, 2021-Dec, question 40).

**Hazzard 8e, examination textbook:** cleanser choice depends on wound condition. Saline is suitable for clean wounds; infected or necrotic wounds may need antiseptics. Saline must not be called a universal gold standard for every wound (pp. 692–693).

**A. Hydrogen peroxide 3%.** Wrong, the textbook says not to use hydrogen peroxide on open wounds (p. 692).
**B. Normal saline, NaCl 0.9%.** Correct, officially accepted. Physiological saline can be used for a clean wound, but the book does not give it universal superiority for every pressure injury (p. 693).
**C. Sterile mineral water.** Wrong, wrong for scoring. Water and saline lack antiseptic activity; these pages do not establish saline’s superiority over water in every situation. Do not invent such a distinction to justify the key (pp. 692–693).
**D. Povidone-iodine 10%.** Wrong, wrong for scoring, but the textbook includes povidone-iodine among antiseptic cleansers and stresses matching treatment to the wound. Exam rejection is not a blanket clinical prohibition (pp. 692–693).

**WHS 2023 update, published in 2024:** evidence favoring one cleanser or technique is limited. The guideline advises against antiseptic cleansing because it damages granulation tissue and also permits tap water. This supports avoiding hydrogen peroxide and povidone-iodine as cleansers, but does not establish saline’s superiority over every alternative; saline remains the official answer.
"Little evidence exists supporting the use of one type of wound cleansing solution or technique for pressure ulcers." (WHS Guideline 3.5, p. 15; PDF p. 10).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 692–693; Gould LJ et al. WHS guidelines for the treatment of pressure ulcers—2023 update. Wound Repair Regen. 2024;32:6–33, Guideline 3.5, p. 15. doi:10.1111/wrr.13130.

explanationSource.status: Official accepted answer first; separately attributed book and secondary sources.

q: מה מהבאים מעלה את הסיכון לאספירציה אחרי הניתוח?
o: כאב לאחר ניתוח
אטלקטזיס לאחר ניתוח
ניתוח אורטופדי
המצאות בקע סרעפתי
explanation:
Hazzard lists **hiatal hernia**, reduced esophageal sphincter tone, delayed gastric emptying, and reflux among factors that may increase perioperative aspiration risk. This supports the hiatal-hernia choice without attributing a detailed anatomical mechanism or anesthesia timing to the page (p. 376).

**A. Postoperative pain.** Wrong, it is not the factor specified in this page’s aspiration-risk list. This does not mean pain should go untreated (p. 376).
**B. Postoperative atelectasis.** Wrong, Hazzard describes atelectasis and aspiration as postoperative pulmonary complications; it does not identify atelectasis as the structural factor increasing aspiration (pp. 375–376).
**C. Orthopedic surgery.** Wrong, this procedure category is not the factor listed among swallowing and esophageal abnormalities increasing aspiration risk; the page does not support choosing it over hiatal hernia (p. 376).
**D. Presence of a hiatal hernia.** Correct, it is explicitly included among factors that may increase perioperative aspiration risk (p. 376).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 375–376.
